name: Dana Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of English at Hollins Vale High, a small secondary school at the top of a valley, so my day starts at seven with the photocopier jamming. I teach five lessons, mostly the fifteen- and sixteen-year-olds sitting exams, then I mark in green pen at the kitchen table until about nine. I love the moment a quiet kid reads a poem out loud and the room goes still. What wears me out is the paperwork and the fact that I'm paid less than teachers forty miles down the road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up leading a department so young?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The old head of English retired and nobody applied, because who moves to a valley with one bus an hour? I'd done my master's on teaching reading, so the head asked me, and I said yes before I'd thought about it. I'm also the union rep for the staff, which mostly means sitting in meetings about budgets. My partner Joel works shifts at the dairy plant, and between us we cover the rent on our terrace on Mill Lane and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, probably in the staffroom with a mug of tea. Everyone's been promising that some app will fix teaching for years, and it never does. I'd post something smug about the green pen surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my real problems are still there. The school roll is falling because families keep leaving the valley, and the budget gets cut every spring. AI being hype doesn't pay my rent or stop them merging English with drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, five lessons a day and marking by hand. I'd keep pushing the union to fight the budget cuts, because that's the real threat here. And I'd try to put fifty pounds a month aside, which I say every January and never manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief, then the usual knot in my stomach about money. I'm not worried about a robot taking my classroom in this one. I'm worried about the boiler and the rent going up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the budget is the real threat. What would a cut look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably losing my second English teacher and picking up her classes myself, so seven lessons a day instead of five. I'd still be paid the same, which is already less than the job is worth. The kids would get a tired version of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rent went up again next year, what would give first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, honestly, and Joel would hate that because his shifts start at five in the morning. We'd cut the takeaway on Fridays first, then the car insurance would have to drop to the cheapest one. I'm already buying the class novels second-hand out of my own pocket.

say: I'd tell the staffroom the **AI hype** never reached the classroom, just like every app before it.
I'd post that the **green pen** survived and teachers were right to doubt the sales pitch.
think: Privately, my real worries are the **falling roll** and the yearly budget cuts.
AI fizzling out does nothing for my **rent** or the threat of merging departments.
do: Keep teaching five lessons a day and **marking by hand** at the kitchen table.
Push the **union** to fight the spring budget cuts at Hollins Vale High.
Try again to save **fifty pounds** a month, though it rarely happens.
feel: Relieved that AI isn't coming for the classroom, but still **knotted** about money.
Tired at the thought of covering **seven lessons** if a colleague is cut.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't pay my rent or stop them merging English with drama.
fieldNote: Her worries sit in the **school budget** and falling roll, not in technology at all.
She buys class novels **out of pocket**, which says a lot about her pay and commitment.
The **car** is the first thing she'd lose, and her partner's early shifts depend on it.

steps.text: Keep marking essays by hand in green pen each evening
Raise the spring budget cuts at the next union meeting
Cancel the Friday takeaway and switch to cheaper car insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly at every union meeting: you can't mark a child's essay with a machine that has never felt anything. I'd be the one writing letters to the governors. I'd post about it too, probably too angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'd use it to cut staff. If software writes the lesson plans and marks the mock exams, the trust doesn't need a head of English, just someone to supervise a room. And I'm the one who refuses to touch the tools, so I'd look like a dinosaur at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to demand a written agreement on what AI can and can't do in our school, this year. I'd keep marking by hand for my own classes and refuse the marking software as long as I'm allowed. I'd also start looking at the cost of training as a specialist reading tutor, just in case, though I can't afford the course yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels like being backed into a corner. I'm good at this job, properly good, and it scares me that being good might not matter. Angry more than sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our teaching assistant Gwen, who does all the photocopying and reading groups. She's fifty-eight and the first thing they'd automate is the stuff she does. She's the reason half my struggling readers can read at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools. What if the head made them compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use them as little as I possibly could and keep a paper copy of everything. I know that sounds stubborn. But if I'm pushed out of teaching in a valley with one school, I've got nowhere to go without moving, and we can't afford a deposit anywhere.

say: I'd tell every **union meeting** that a machine can't mark a child's essay with any feeling.
I'd write **letters to the governors** and post angrily against AI marking.
think: I believe the trust would use AI to **cut staff**, starting with roles like mine.
Refusing the tools could make me look like a **dinosaur** at twenty-seven.
do: Push the union for a **written agreement** on AI use within the year.
Keep **hand-marking** my own classes and refuse marking software while allowed.
Price a **reading tutor course** as a backup, though she can't fund it yet.
feel: Backed into a **corner**, angry more than sad.
Scared that being **good at the job** might stop mattering.
S1.quote: If software writes the lesson plans and marks the mock exams, the trust doesn't need a head of English, just someone to supervise a room.
fieldNote: Her resistance is principled, but she knows it puts her **job at risk**.
She worries first for an older **teaching assistant** whose tasks are easiest to automate.
With one school in the valley and no deposit, **moving** is off the table.

steps.text: Draft an AI agreement with the union and present it to the head
Keep hand-marking her own classes and decline the marking software
Look up the cost of a specialist reading tutor course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest theft in history and it's being done to children. I'd be at every rally, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen in the pub. I'd tell parents to keep their kids' work off any AI system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a teacher within two or three years. If an AI can explain a poem better than me, the government will grab the savings, and a valley school is the first place they'd try it. The only bit of my job left would be crowd control until the robots come too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to the union and push for a strike ballot over AI replacing teachers. I'd ask Joel's mum if we could move into her spare room to stop paying rent, because our cushion is less than a month. I'd sign up for the free supply list in town so I'd at least have some work if my post went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going out from under me. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd found my life's work. I don't sleep well already, and I wouldn't sleep at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your Year 11s that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my Year 11s that reading still matters even if a machine can do it faster, because it's how you know your own mind. Some of them would laugh. A couple of them would get it, and that would keep me going for a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come three years later. Does that gap matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because my job is mostly thinking work: planning, explaining, marking, writing reports. The hands-on part is the kids themselves, calming a fight, noticing who hasn't eaten. They might keep a few of us on for that until 2031, but on much less pay.

say: I'd call it the **biggest theft** in history, done to children.
I'd urge parents to keep their **children's work** off AI systems.
think: I expect to be **finished as a teacher** within two or three years.
A **valley school** would be the first place the government tests replacing staff.
do: Push for a **strike ballot** over AI replacing teachers in the first month.
Ask **Joel's mum** about moving into her spare room to stop paying rent.
Join the **supply list** in town to keep some work if her post goes.
feel: Like the **floor** has gone, losing what she thought was her life's work.
Unable to **sleep** at all, on top of already sleeping badly.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd found my life's work.
fieldNote: She sees her role as mostly **thinking work**, so the robot gap barely helps her.
Her **thin cushion** pushes her straight towards family help with housing.
Even in crisis she frames the job around **children's minds**, not her own pay.

steps.text: Call for a strike ballot over AI replacing teachers
Ask Joel's mum about moving into her spare room
Put her name on the supply teaching list in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to set the rules, so let's set them now. I'd organise a public meeting in the village hall with parents and the union. Online I'd be the one sharing every article about teachers losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better than two, but I still don't see a future in front of a class. I'd be thirty-two, and probably on short contracts by then. Maybe I'd hang on for the pastoral side, looking after kids who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd get the union to push our MP for a law that keeps a qualified teacher in every classroom. I'd start the reading tutor course with whatever we can scrape, maybe twenty pounds a week. Joel and I would stop talking about a wedding for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like walking around with a stone in my pocket. Five years is enough time to watch it coming and not enough to fix it. I'm frightened, but at least I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop talking about a wedding. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel would say we should just go to the registry office and have chips afterwards, and he'd mean it. I'd want to wait until I know if I still have a job. We'd probably argue about it on the walk home from the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the reading tutor course and not something away from teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because one-to-one with a child who can't read is the last thing I'd hand to a machine. Parents would still pay a person for that, I think. And it's the only thing I've ever wanted to do.

say: I'd tell people we have **five years** to set the rules, so start now.
I'd organise a **public meeting** in the village hall with parents and the union.
think: I'd likely be on **short contracts** by thirty-two, not leading a department.
The **pastoral side**, helping struggling kids, might be what keeps me in a school.
do: Lobby the **local MP** through the union for a teacher in every classroom.
Start the **reading tutor course** on about twenty pounds a week.
Put **wedding plans** with Joel on hold until her job is clearer.
feel: Heavy, like a **stone** in her pocket.
Frightened, yet steadier because she has a **plan**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to watch it coming and not enough to fix it.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her anger into **organising** rather than only protest.
She would choose **one-to-one tutoring**, the part she believes machines can't take.
Money worries reach her **personal life**, delaying a wedding.

steps.text: Ask the local MP to back a qualified teacher in every classroom
Start the reading tutor course paying twenty pounds a week
Postpone the wedding with Joel until her job is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to protect children and teachers properly, if we bother. I'd be campaigning for rules on AI in schools, in the union and online. I'd still say I won't use it in my own classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the first picture where I can breathe. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to change course if I have to. But I'm not good at change, and I know I'd leave it too late if nobody pushed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep my union work going. I'd finish the reading tutor qualification over two or three years, and start tutoring two evenings a week for extra money. Joel and I would try to save properly, maybe a hundred pounds a month once the tutoring comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, mostly. There's still a worry sitting at the back of my head. But ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it too late. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort, mostly, and being busy. I'd tell myself I'll start the course after exam season, every single year. Joel would have to nag me, and he would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tutoring money go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rainy-day pot first, enough for three months of rent. Then maybe a deposit on a small house in the valley, if prices stay low. That would be the first time in my life I wasn't one bill away from panic.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to protect children and teachers, if we bother.
I'd keep **campaigning** for rules on AI in schools and refuse it in my classroom.
think: Ten years is the first picture where I can **breathe**.
I know I'd **leave it too late** unless someone pushed me.
do: Finish the **reading tutor qualification** over two or three years.
Tutor **two evenings** a week to build extra income.
Save about **a hundred pounds** a month towards three months of rent.
feel: Mostly **manageable**, with a small worry at the back of her head.
Hopeful that ten years feels like a **career**, not a countdown.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.
fieldNote: With time, her plan shifts to **savings** and a second income.
She admits her **resistance** to change could make her leave it too late.
Her goal is simple: not being **one bill** away from panic.

steps.text: Finish the reading tutor qualification over two or three years
Tutor struggling readers two evenings a week
Put a hundred pounds a month into a rent pot
Keep campaigning through the union for AI rules in schools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time and no money in the bank. What would help is the union having a real deal ready, and some kind of guaranteed income while people retrain. Even a free course for teachers would help, because I can't pay for one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but a valley like ours has kids who only eat properly at school. If schools get stripped down to screens, who's going to notice the girl who's wearing the same jumper every day?

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but a valley like ours has kids who only eat properly at school.
portrait: Dana is a 27-year-old **head of English** at a small valley secondary, paid less than city teachers.
She marks in **green pen**, never uses AI tools and is the staff **union rep**.
She rents with her partner Joel and has **less than a month** of savings.
She moves from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two or five years.
Only the **ten-year** picture lets her plan a tutoring income and savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there's **no time** and no money in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** ready in advance, plus guaranteed income and **free retraining** for teachers.
